We examined dragging performance and subjective workload using controller-based ray casting in two repeated-measures experiments with 12 participants each. Experiment 1 used curvilinear measurements, whereas Experiment 2 used angular measurements. Both manipulated display curvature, viewing depth, target amplitude and width. The results show that, compared with flat displays, curved displays with specific curvature settings yielded shorter movement times, lower error rates, and lower subjective workload. Increasing depth reduced movement time under curvilinear measurement but increased it under angular measurement. We further evaluated existing Fitts’ law adaptations and proposed an extension of the two-part model that incorporates display curvature. These findings inform the design and modeling of dragging interactions on curved VR displays.

This study investigates human–AI collaboration and strategic decision-making in UAE government institutions, examining how artificial intelligence is transforming leadership practices, decision processes and human judgement. Although AI is integral to the UAE’s digital government transformation, existing research has focused mainly on technological adoption, organisational performance and digital transformation, leaving limited understanding of how human–AI collaboration reconfigures strategic decision-making and leadership responsibilities. The study addresses this gap by examining the relationship between human judgement and AI-enabled decision support, the effects of collaboration on strategic decision-making and organisational transformation, and emerging leadership challenges in AI-enabled governance. An exploratory qualitative research design was employed, drawing on academic literature, policy documents, official government publications and other documentary sources. The data were analysed thematically, guided by Dynamic Capabilities Theory, to identify patterns related to collaboration, decision-making, leadership transformation and human judgement. Findings show that AI is moving strategic decision-making towards collaborative arrangements in which AI provides analytical capabilities, predictive insights and decision support, while human leaders retain responsibility for contextual interpretation, ethical reasoning and final judgement. The study contributes by extending understanding of AI-enabled leadership through a human–AI collaboration perspective, demonstrating how technological capabilities and human judgement can be integrated within government decision processes. It concludes that effective AI governance requires complementarity rather than leadership displacement. Future research should examine these dynamics through empirical studies involving government leaders and employees across different UAE institutions and comparative public-sector contexts and broader institutional outcomes. The study recommends strengthening AI literacy, leadership capabilities, institutional readiness and responsible governance.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Background Agricultural workers face some of the highest suicide rates in the United States, yet limited research has examined suicide among immigrant and migrant farmworkers (IMFs), a population recognized as particularly vulnerable within occupational health surveillance priorities. This study examined circumstances contributing to suicide among IMFs and compared these to circumstances among U.S.-born farmworkers using National Violent Death Reporting System (NVDRS) data. Methods This multiple methods study used NVDRS data from 2013 to 2023, restricted to decedents in agricultural worker occupations (SOC Minor Group 45–2000) who died by suicide. Decedents were classified as IMFs (foreign-born) or U.S.-born based on birthplace. Bivariate analyses examined associations between nativity and reported circumstances preceding suicide, followed by multivariable logistic regression adjusted for age, sex, race, ethnicity, marital status, and education. A single-author qualitative analysis of investigative narratives, using an iterative inductive coding process with peer debriefing as a rigor check, identified themes describing IMF suicide circumstances. Results Of 1,162 decedents, 17% ( n = 201) were foreign-born. IMFs were older, more likely male, more likely Hispanic, and had lower educational attainment than U.S.-born decedents. IMFs were less likely to die by firearm (22% vs. 57%) and more likely to die by hanging/strangulation/suffocation (64% vs. 30%). In adjusted analysis, Hispanic ethnicity (OR = 0.014), older age (OR = 0.961), and being married (OR = 0.366) were associated with lower odds, while firearm method (OR = 2.126) was associated with higher odds, of U.S.-born status. Investigative documentation completeness did not differ significantly by nativity. Qualitative analysis identified four themes: stigma and avoidance of mental health care; violent and conflictual intimate relationships; substance use and associated familial shame; and immigration-related vulnerability and compounded isolation. Conclusion IMFs experience intersectional stressors—including immigration-related vulnerability, stigma, and isolation—that shape suicide risk in ways distinct from U.S.-born farmworkers, and that align with constructs of thwarted belongingness and perceived burdensomeness from the Interpersonal-Psychological Theory of Suicide. Predominant use of hanging/strangulation among IMFs highlights limitations of conventional lethal means restriction strategies for this population. Culturally responsive, community-based, and workplace interventions—including stigma reduction, social connection programming, and multilingual lethal means safety messaging—are needed to address suicide risk among this underrecognized and vulnerable occupational group.

Dermatitis is a common occupational health concern among agricultural workers, who are frequently exposed to environmental irritants, pesticides, fertilizers, plants, and prolonged sunlight exposure. Inadequate knowledge and suboptimal personal hygiene practices may further increase the risk of persistent skin problems. This study aimed to describe the application of personal hygiene health education, combined with family-supported mentoring, to address a knowledge deficit in a farmer with dermatitis. A case study design was conducted in the working area of the Padang Community Health Center involving a 53-year-old sugarcane farm laborer and her family. The intervention was implemented over seven consecutive days. It consisted of four visits, two structured educational sessions focused on recognizing dermatitis and appropriate personal hygiene practices, and continuous family-supported mentoring. Knowledge was assessed using pre-intervention and post-intervention questionnaires, while relevant behavioral responses were documented throughout the intervention period. The participant demonstrated several misconceptions about dermatitis and suboptimal hygiene practices at baseline, including delayed bathing, inconsistent handwashing, and reusing field clothing. Following the intervention, the knowledge score increased from 72.5 to 90, indicating improved understanding of dermatitis and recommended personal hygiene practices. Family-supported educational mentoring was associated with improved knowledge and may represent a feasible nursing approach to strengthening self-management of dermatitis among agricultural workers. Larger studies using validated instruments, comparative designs, and longer follow-up periods are required to evaluate the effectiveness and sustainability of this intervention.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) foundation models have scaled rapidly to enhance manipulation performance and generalizability, but this scaling incurs high computational costs that render real-world deployment increasingly challenging. Existing approaches typically mitigate this issue by designing smaller architectures or reducing the iterative denoising steps in flow-based policies. In this work, we propose FastOPD, a foundation-to-lightweight VLA framework that enables the practical deployment of large-scale VLAs through efficient on-policy distillation. Specifically, FastOPD adapts a flow map for single-state teacher supervision and combines it with a self-consistency objective to construct a compact student that learns the teacher dynamics. Furthermore, we theoretically demonstrate that minimizing this objective allows the distilled student to recover a distribution on par with that induced by an ideal few-step teacher model. We evaluate FastOPD across diverse foundation policies in simulation and real-world experiments. On LIBERO, FastOPD retains 84% of the performance of $π_{0.5}$ with only two inference steps, reducing inference latency by 78.1% while outperforming existing few-step distillation baselines in average success rate. With LingBot-VLA as the teacher, FastOPD improves the single-step success rate over the base student by 15.9 percentage points on RoboTwin 2.0. We further demonstrate its applicability to a World Action Model (WAM) and deploy a compact student distilled from MolmoAct2 on a real robot.

Abstract Interdisciplinary clinical boards (ICB) on chronic inflammatory diseases discuss complicated and multidisciplinary cases with inflammatory conditions among experts in their discipline. Medically specialized large language models (LLMs) are finding increasingly widespread use among physicians to answer clinical questions. LLMs offer the potential to close the gap between rapidly expanding medical knowledge and limited time of physicians by providing evidence-based summaries to clinical questions and enable “real-time” literature search. However, it is unclear if LLMs can be implemented in clinical routine of ICB. In this prospective study, 100 consecutive real-world cases were discussed in our ICB. Each case was first discussed independently of the LLM and a preliminary recommendation was documented. The clinical question was then entered in the LLM “OpenEvidence”, the answer was reviewed by the board with the opportunity to add aspects not previously raised, and the recommendation was subsequently confirmed as final. Each participating expert evaluated the answer of the LLM using a questionnaire comprising eight Likert scale (1–5) items and one free-text item. Two physicians, blinded to each other, additionally evaluated outputs for their agreement with the board’s decision. The same cases were evaluated after prompt optimization at two different time points. The 100 discussed cases resulted in 759 rater-case evaluations. A mean of 2.3 specialties were directly involved in each case. The highest score was achieved by the item “OpenEvidence provided clinically relevant information for this case.” (4.06). Recommendation for future use achieved a mean score of 3.95. Complete agreement of the LLM answer with the final recommendation of the ICB was rated in 40.2% and 50.5% of all evaluable cases ( n = 97) by the two raters. When restricted to consensus cases, i.e. cases rated identically by both raters ( n = 62 of 97), complete agreement was 51.6%. Outputs after prompt optimization tended to be associated with higher agreement, but did not reach statistical significance. Outputs were not stable over time. The integration of OpenEvidence into an ICB was feasible and was perceived as useful by the participating specialists, with partial or complete concordance with the final board recommendation in the majority of evaluable cases. As the study did not assess patient outcomes, clinical harm or hallucinations, no conclusions on patient safety can be drawn. The LLM was naturally limited by the information provided in the prompt. Inadequate questions or missing information led to suboptimal answers, highlighting the importance of identifying and including relevant information beforehand. Expert oversight remains essential. Model drift of LLMs may outweigh prompt optimization.

This paper presents a complete framework for feature-driven Android malware detection that combines predictive modeling with explainable artificial intelligence to improve classification accuracy, interpretability, and operational dependability. The system initiates by examining network-flow metrics, including Source Port (SP), Initial Window Bytes Forward (IW), packet rates, and user activity indicators, derived from a publicly accessible dataset including 355,630 cases across four classifications: Adware, Scareware, SMS malware, and benign. Feature preprocessing utilizes the Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) analysis to eliminate multicollinearity to discern the most important variables, hence assuring a non-redundant and highly relevant feature collection. Subsequently, Gradient Boosting Classifier (XGBC) and Decision Tree Classifier (DTC) are augmented with metaheuristic optimization algorithms, Tailor Optimization Algorithm (TOA) and Spotted Deer Optimization Algorithm (SDOA), to boost convergence, stability, and generalization. Model interpretability is attained by Delta-XAI, which identifies SP, IW, and User Interaction/Write operations as the principal features, collectively representing approximately 80% of the explanatory power of the top features. Assessment by five-fold cross-validation indicates that the XGBC+TOA (XGTO) configuration attains an overall accuracy of 98.0%, exhibiting excellent precision and Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC), surpassing all other models. This framework combines feature-centric selection, enhanced learning, and explainable AI to deliver a dependable, interpretable, and pragmatic approach for identifying Android malware, thereby connecting data-driven analysis with practical cybersecurity implementations.

Foundation models have shown remarkable generalization ability for few-shot learning (FSL). However, their potential for remote sensing scene classification has not been fully explored. Existing methods mainly adapt a single vision–language model and seldom exploit the complementary strengths of different foundation models. Moreover, the inconsistency between visual and textual representations limits the effectiveness of cross-modal learning under limited supervision. To address these issues, we propose a framework for few-shot remote sensing scene classification leveraging collaboration of foundation models. Specifically, the proposed framework integrates a large language model, a text-to-image diffusion model, and a vision–language model to enrich class semantics, synthesize category-related training samples, and learn transferable visual-textual representations. Furthermore, a Deep Cross-modal Alignment (DCA) module is developed to improve feature consistency across modalities. The DCA module incorporates multi-scale visual features, lightweight adapters, and a contrastive learning objective to obtain more discriminative task-adaptive representations. Extensive experiments on 12 remote sensing scene classification datasets under various few-shot settings demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves competitive performance compared with existing prompt learning and efficient parameter tuning methods, with consistent improvements observed on average across the evaluated datasets. Recent multimodal large language models evaluated in the zero-shot setting are additionally reported as references, while the 2-shot results of our method illustrate the performance when limited labeled data are available. This comparison provides a broader view of the trade-offs between label availability, classification accuracy, and inference cost across the two paradigms.

The superficial white matter (SWM), a critical brain region for cognition across the lifespan and brain disease, contains abundant short-range association fibers whose organization remains incompletely characterized, in part because the short trajectories and highly variable cortical folding make correspondence across individuals challenging. Anatomically corresponding connections may vary in spatial location across individuals and therefore may not be adequately defined by geometric proximity alone. We introduce FiberGeoText (FGT), a vision-language model (VLM) for organizing short-range superficial white matter (SWM) streamlines reconstructed from ultra-high-resolution diffusion MRI into population-level clusters. FGT jointly represents three complementary properties of each streamline: its three-dimensional trajectory, its cortical anatomical context, and its shape. Cortical endpoint information from multiple parcellation schemes is expressed as text and encoded using a pretrained large language model (LLM), enabling heterogeneous anatomical descriptions to contribute to a common continuous representation. We evaluated FGT on acquired submillimeter 0.76 mm diffusion MRI data. Compared with state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods, FGT produced substantially greater cortical parcel coherence, within-cluster shape consistency, cluster-size consistency, and cross-subject correspondence. The trained model also generalizes well to unseen subjects with an average of 96.7% of the 5,000 learned clusters recovered, and high consistency of cluster structure between training and testing data. Together, these findings demonstrate that integrating geometric, anatomical, and shape information by learning multimodal deep embeddings with a VLM model enables robust learning of population-consistent SWM organization despite interindividual anatomical variability.

Conventional fire-safety awareness campaigns built on brochures, leaflets, and instructional videos have shown limited success in developing transferable hazard-recognition skills, and simply moving this content into a virtual reality (VR) headset does not resolve the problem. This Project Report synthesizes fifteen cross-cutting lessons learned from a three-phase FireGuard case study conducted in Dubai and Sharjah, spanning a 149-resident needs-assessment survey, an expert-validated True-Context (TContext) game design, and an 80-participant controlled experiment in which the contextual group achieved higher learning gains and outperformed a non-contextual VR baseline on usability, engagement, and motivation. Rather than presenting new experimental data, this report integrates findings from three reported phases into a single cross-phase account and an accompanying six-layer evaluation architecture. The fifteen lessons are organized into three clusters. The Phase 1 survey yields three diagnostic lessons that show a clear distinction. Awareness is not preparedness. Passive delivery persists for cost reasons, not effectiveness. Training access remains structurally unequal and employer-dependent. The TContext framework and Phase 2 expert review yield a further set of design lessons: Passive content does not become contextual simply by appearing inside a headset, Contextual design - more than immersion alone, was associated with the larger learning gains observed. These design lessons also point to the need for explicit temporal and situational escalation. Distributed situational awareness and progressive interactivity should be built into scenario design. Gamification should function as a teaching tool rather than a descriptive layer. Structured, multi-domain expert review before user trials is likewise associated with reduced redesign costs. Phase 3 and the integrative discussion yield five lessons on evaluation and deployment. Balance interaction realism against accessibility for non-technical users. Sustain motivation through real-time, scenario-anchored feedback. Isolate the independent variable through rigorous experimental design. Adopt a six-layer evaluation architecture, spanning reach to durable behaviour change. Data quality is shaped through field logistics and human factors. Together, these fifteen lessons offer practical, theory-grounded guidance. They are intended for researchers, safety educators, and policymakers designing similar VR interventions in other high-density, multilingual urban settings. However, their transferability beyond the present study has not been directly tested.

Background: GenAI has entered education rapidly, intensifying debates about pedagogy, authority, ethics, and disciplinary integrity. In history education, these tensions are especially pronounced because GenAI can support access, scaffolding, and experimentation while also flattening interpretation, obscuring evidence, and reproducing dominant narratives. Focus of Study: This conceptual paper introduces technocuriosity as a methodological and pedagogical stance for history educators, teacher educators, and researchers engaging GenAI in practice. Situated in conversation with postdigital and speculative scholarship in education, technocuriosity approaches GenAI as an emergent, sociotechnical problem space best studied through recursive, critical experimentation. Research Design: We develop a four-part framework centered on configuration, figures, liveness, and speculative futures, and use these layers to trace the conditions under which GenAI is introduced, negotiated, resisted, or incorporated in history classrooms. We then outline the methodological commitments that follow from this stance, including recursive prompting, persona work, shadow archives, and classroom experimentation. Conclusions: Technocuriosity offers a way to engage GenAI with curiosity disciplined by historical thinking, ethical scrutiny, and attention to power, while keeping inquiry, interpretation, and evidence at the center of history education.

Critic-free reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT) for agentic large language models is often done through GRPO-style methods, which compute a group baseline over repeated rollouts to reduce target variance. However, this setup is ill-suited to agents acting in stateful environments such as live services or security sandboxes, where repeated rollouts are impractical to obtain and aggressive updates entrench the noise of long, sparsely verified trajectories. We propose \textit{Follow the Winners} (FTW), a critic-free policy-learning algorithm that adapts the cross-entropy method to RFT, replacing group rollouts with an ordinal filter on replay-buffer samples that yields polynomial concentration in the order statistic of returns. We derive FTW through a control-as-inference lens, which also recovers GRPO and DPO as specific modelling choices, identifying GRPO as risk-neutral while DPO and FTW share a bounded risk-seeking offset that FTW controls. We identify this offset as an inherent trade-off of variance reduction through ordinal filters on samples, whereas a critic model induces a different trade-off between bias and variance. Scaled to agentic LLM post-training, FTW matches GRPO and PPO on Sokoban and Search-R1 baselines, showing a viable trade-off from a value model or group rollouts to CPU memory.

Suppressing a small set of routed experts can weaken the safety behavior of a sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language model without retraining. Which experts to suppress is therefore a security question, and the usual answer is activation frequency, but frequency measures use, not influence. We test an alternative: router-gradient sensitivity, the sensitivity of the sequence loss to the gate weights that select an expert. Across five MoE architectures, we rank experts by each signal on 500 benign and 500 malicious prompts and measure refusal on 100 held-out malicious prompts under two budgets: equal expert counts and equal nominal malicious routing traffic (1%-5%). Under each of the two budgets, router-gradient selection reduces refusals more than activation in 24 of 25 conditions, and more than a ten-trial random mean in all 25. The largest effect is in OLMoE, where refusals fall from 34 to 9 of 100 prompts (73.53% relative) with no degraded outputs, indicating substantive compliance rather than broken generation. After matching expert counts in every layer, gradient selection still produces greater refusal reduction than activation in 23 of 25 conditions, with two ties. An exploratory cross-model analysis links larger malicious-versus-benign concentration gaps to greater peak gradient effects (rho = 0.90; exact two-sided p = 0.083, n = 5). Together, the results support gradient selection under the tested budgets.

General-purpose Text-to-SQL systems achieve strong performance on academic benchmarks like Spider and BIRD, where schemas are relatively shallow and column values are often human readable. In production financial databases, where concepts are stored as opaque integer keys rather than human-readable strings, these methods fall below 50%, as even simple queries require multiple joins and filter predicates reference opaque IDs. We present Financial LINking Text-to-SQL (FLINT), a domain-specialized Text-to-SQL system that closes this gap through three key components: (1) a lookup agent that dynamically resolves natural-language concepts to question-specific reference table constraints, (2) embedding-based retrieval of structurally similar query templates from a compact, expert-authored bank, and (3) schema linking that prunes a large table schema to the relevant subset by traversing foreign-key chains, rather than relying on name similarity alone. We evaluate on two datasets totaling 359 questions over production financial schemas. FLINT outperforms various state-of-the-art baselines using the same LLM. The system is deployed in production as part of a financial data retrieval service.

Corporate governance has traditionally assumed that important company decisions are made by human directors, managers, and officers who can be questioned about the reasons for their choices. Artificial intelligence is changing that assumption. AI systems are now used to analyse markets, assess risk, screen employees, detect fraud, forecast demand, recommend investments, and in some settings take actions with little or no human intervention. The legal problem is not simply whether a company may use AI. It is whether existing rules on directors’ duties can still allocate responsibility when an important corporate decision is partly or largely produced by an algorithm. This paper examines that problem mainly through Indian company law, with comparative reference to Delaware, the United Kingdom, the European Union, the OECD and the United States National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST). Section 166 of the Companies Act, 2013 requires directors to act in good faith, exercise due and reasonable care, skill and diligence, and use independent judgment. These duties remain relevant when AI is used. The difficulty is that the traditional idea of a director as the person who gathers information and then exercises judgment does not fit neatly where an AI system filters information, recommends an outcome, or executes the decision itself. The paper argues that AI should not become a legal excuse for directors, but directors should also not become automatic guarantors of every error made by a system they did not design or operate. Liability should instead be linked to the degree of AI autonomy, the importance of the decision, the quality of human oversight, the foreseeability of the risk, and the ability of the company and its directors to intervene. The paper proposes an AI Corporate Responsibility Framework with four levels of AI use: assistive, delegated, supervised autonomous, and high-autonomy decision systems. For each level, it proposes a different combination of board oversight, documentation, testing, human review, vendor responsibility, and director liability. The central conclusion is that the duty of directors should evolve into a clear duty of AI oversight. This duty would require directors to understand the material AI systems used by the company, identify significant risks, establish suitable controls, monitor performance, keep records of important AI-supported decisions, and intervene when a system presents a serious or foreseeable risk. Such a framework protects the basic principle of director accountability while recognising that modern corporate decisions may be produced through a network of directors, employees, software providers, data sources, and autonomous systems.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Adaptive LLM reinforcement-learning post-training changes multiple training actuators online, including rollout temperature, group size, clipping, KL regularization, verifier allocation, and update budget. Three coupled issues remain unresolved. A future-risk model trained from behavior trajectories need not estimate the risk induced by the controller that will be deployed; a score calibrated on logged state-action pairs can become miscalibrated after selective action choice; and independent per-resource minimum costs do not in general certify a feasible multi-resource continuation. We introduce FSPO, a feedback-state controller for budgeted LLM RL post-training that addresses these issues jointly. FSPO learns a policy-consistent risk-to-go model whose Bellman target follows the same frozen controller used for future decisions, together with a long-horizon utility model. Decision-conditioned trajectory calibration (DCTC) calibrates risk on cross-fitted trajectories generated by actions selected by provisional controllers. A Pareto resource continuation certificate (PRCC) admits an action only when a non-dominated cumulative reservation remains feasible over the residual horizon. Under a matched GRPO resource envelope, FSPO reaches 66.11% held-out and 59.43% OOD accuracy, compared with 64.47% and 57.03% for PB2, the strongest evaluated adaptive baseline. Three paired training seeds give gains of +2.42 and +3.19 percentage points over the contextual bandit on held-out and OOD evaluation. Under high behavior-deployment mismatch, policy-consistent risk lowers selected-decision ECE from 0.108 to 0.053; DCTC lowers it from 0.039 to 0.022 at matched acceptance; PRCC removes false-feasible admissions on an 18-action catalog ($0.197\rightarrow0.000$); and enabling all three components reduces trajectory failure from 0.181 to 0.083 in a factorial ablation.

Generative artificial intelligence (Gen AI) is rapidly becoming the dominating force in this new age, despite the fact that Generation Z has played a significant role in defining the digital culture that exists today. As a consequence of the exponential rise of digital technology, this shift of power has occurred. The generation of artificial intelligence ushers in a paradigm shift toward machines having the capacity to build, learn, and evolve on their own. This is in contrast to the well-deserved reputation that Generation Z has for technical aptitude, innovation, and dependency on digital platforms for expression and communication. The ways in which Gen AI is influencing decision- making, education, creative industries, work processes, and social behaviour are discussed in depth in this article. In this in-depth examination, you will learn about the benefits and drawbacks of the digital identity developed by Generation Z in connection to the autonomous intelligence developed by Generation AI. According to the findings of the study, the transition from Generation Z to Gen AI is more than just a shift in technology; it also represents a reevaluation of human obligations in the digital age, the nature of digital dominance, and the path that innovation will take. The purpose of this study is to highlight the ways in which Gen AI is influencing the next digital age, following in the footsteps of Generation Z. Generation Z's innovation, social media, and connection were the primary factors that contributed to the formation of digital culture. Generative artificial intelligence, on the other hand, ushers in autonomic technology that is capable of cognition, creation, and operation. This transformation, which signals a new age in which AI meets human digital skills, is expected to bring about significant changes in a variety of domains, including education, work, communication and society as a whole.
topics: Interdisciplinary Studies: Technology, Society, and Humanities

documents.abstract: The gaps for Occupational Health and Safety (OH&S) performance management in the context of Small-Scale Contractors (SSCs) for developing countries from the reviewed literature are examined in this chapter. Two essential dimensions to OH&S performance, that is, employee well-being and provision of OH&S services, found to be often neglected in most existing frameworks, have been examined. The chapter states that sustainable OH&S performance is attained once well-being programmes that address stress, mental health, and the socio-economic challenges are considered together with more accessible, structured OH&S services where there are constrained resources. Anchoring from the International Labour Organisation (ILO) and World Health Organisation (WHO) standards and the United Nations (UN) Sustainable Development Goals, the discussions in this chapter depict the effects of inadequate employee well-being, which lead to absenteeism, unsafe practices, and reduced productivity. In the same vein, the availability of employee well-being significantly strengthens safety outcomes by providing for targeted interventions such as wellness programmes, counselling, ergonomic design, and stress risk assessment. Further, Affective Events Theory, the Job Demands-Resources model, and the Social Capital Theory are applied as theoretical perspectives to contextualise employee well-being and OH&S service provision as OH&S performance management determinants. In conclusion, the chapter accentuates the significance of integrating employee well-being and OH&S service provision into the OH&S performance management framework for SSCs in developing economies to improve the safety of workers, increase productivity, and enhance competitiveness.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: In most developing countries, the majority of enterprises that constitute the small-scale contractors (SSCs) play a significant role in the construction industry, even though they are vulnerable to challenges related to occupational health and safety (OH&S). The SSCs in these regions record inordinately high rates of accidents and fatalities, which are attributed to inadequate compliance with regulatory requirements, constrained financial resources, insufficient expertise, inadequate training, and ineffective communication. These factors often lead to unreported or underreported incidents and the absence of systematic risk assessments being conducted, causing ineffective interventions and biased data. Further, bad working conditions and poorly paid and physically demanding construction projects lead to negative attitudes, thus exacerbating OH&S risks. This chapter stresses the significance of client-contractor collaboration in ensuring safety culture and the adoption of performance indicators, which are fundamental in reducing risks and optimising OH&S outcomes. The chapter gives a background on the framework developed to enhance SSCs’ capabilities in improving OH&S performance to mitigate incidents and cultivate a culture of compliance. Practical guidance for policymakers, government institutions, and non-governmental organisations (NGOs) is provided in the framework for strengthening SSCs’ capabilities of fostering safer workplaces that promote sustainable construction practices in the sub-Saharan Africa region and beyond.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: ABSTRACT Background The integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) into creative writing is a growing trend. However, few studies have examined primary school students' interactions with GenAI alongside their writing experiences and resulting writing products. Objectives This study compared creative writing performance, writing self‐efficacy, and flow state across GenAI‐supported, peer‐collaborative and individual writing conditions. It also descriptively examined patterns of student–AI interaction during the writing activity. Methods An experiment involved 78 primary school students in China assigned to three conditions: GenAI‐supported writing ( n = 20), peer collaboration ( n = 38; 19 pairs), and individual writing ( n = 20). Results and Conclusions Students in the GenAI‐supported writing group obtained higher creative writing performance scores than those in the peer‐collaborative and individual writing groups. Interaction analysis showed that students mainly used GenAI to generate and elaborate ideas. Among episodes with observable uptake, adapted or selective incorporation was more common than direct incorporation, and no complete GenAI response was reproduced verbatim. In addition, students in the GenAI‐supported writing group also reported higher writing self‐efficacy than those in the individual writing group, although the difference from the peer‐collaborative writing group was not significant. However, they reported the lowest flow state. Writing self‐efficacy was positively associated with creative writing performance, whereas no significant association between flow state and creative writing performance was observed in this sample. These findings suggest that GenAI may serve as a resource for developing ideas in primary school creative writing.

With the advent of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI), the talent acquisition process is transforming, impacting every stage from sourcing jobs to creating job descriptions to parsing candidate resumes to assessing skills and even the interview process. This process can be enhanced by using large language models (LLMs) and advanced machine learning tools. To simplify the process by using language processing (NLP) and advanced machine learning. Recruitment: Find the right candidate for the right role and reduce recruitment costs; Match candidates to roles, reduce recruitment costs, and support data-driven hiring decisions. The quick adoption of GenAI in hiring has led to worries about algorithmic bias, data privacy, explainability, transparency, cybersecurity, regulatory compliance, lack of trust and transparency in recruitment practices, and accountability.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) has created new avenues for the commercial sexual exploitation of children through the creation or manipulation of sexually explicit images using a child's likeness. Such images constitute a form of child sexual abuse material (CSAM), including when they are generated or manipulated without physical contact with the child. Because this abuse may occur without the child's awareness, it can complicate recognition, disclosure, and intervention while contributing to ongoing psychological harm. When such content is produced, distributed, or monetized in exchange for anything of value, it may also constitute commercial sexual exploitation of children (CSEC), a term commonly used to describe child sex trafficking. Healthcare providers play an important role in identifying possible GAI child sexual abuse material (GAI-CSAM), supporting affected children and caregivers, and incorporating digital safety into routine care. This article highlights clinical considerations for pediatric, primary care, and mental health settings, including developmentally appropriate assessment of online experiences, caregiver education, trauma-informed response, and multidisciplinary collaboration. As generative technologies evolve, clinician awareness is essential to strengthen prevention, early intervention, and responses to technology-facilitated exploitation.

Amidst the context of digital transformation and the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence, moral education for university students must go beyond merely shaping character and personality; it must also address the requirements for professional ethics and responsibility within the digital environment. This study focuses on clarifying moral education based on Ho Chi Minh's ideology and the significance of applying these values to the development of highquality human resources among students at nonpublic universities. The research employs methods such as document analysis, analysis and synthesis, comparison and contrast, and systematization. The findings indicate that standards—such as loyalty to the country and devotion to the people; diligence, thrift, integrity, uprightness, and absolute impartiality; and love for humanity—along with principles like aligning words with deeds, balancing construction with destruction, and lifelong moral cultivation, remain valuable in guiding students during the digital era. The study proposes solutions regarding the innovation of educational content and methods, the creation of a digital ethical environment, and the strengthening of coordination among universities, families, businesses, and society. These measures aim to help shape students who possess moral character, professional expertise, digital competence, professional responsibility, and a spirit of dedication, thereby meeting the demands for high-quality human resource development.

The Global Police Operational Competence and Education Framework (G‑POCEF) is a multidisciplinary conceptual systems framework that seeks to develop a universal architecture for understanding, developing, assessing, and sustaining police competence, professional performance, organisational capability, leadership effectiveness, legitimacy, and public safety across jurisdictions. Policing systems operate within highly diverse legal, cultural, social, political, economic, and organisational environments. Despite substantial variation in laws, governance structures, training systems, community expectations, and operational demands, police organisations worldwide face common challenges involving public safety, ethical decision making, authority, accountability, legitimacy, operational effectiveness, workforce development, leadership, and organisational adaptation. G‑POCEF seeks to identify and examine the foundational principles that may contribute to effective policing across these diverse contexts. The framework draws upon literature from policing studies, criminology, educational science, psychology, decision science, organisational behaviour, leadership research, systems theory, public administration, human factors science, resilience research, comparative institutional analysis, sociology, ethics, governance studies, and public policy. The objective is to develop an integrated architecture capable of explaining how police competence emerges, develops, and functions within complex and dynamic operational environments. G‑POCEF proposes that police competence cannot be understood solely as the possession of isolated knowledge, skills, or professional qualifications. Rather, the framework conceptualises competence as an emergent property arising from interactions among multiple domains, including legal competence, ethical competence, cognitive competence, decision-making competence, communication competence, tactical competence, emotional competence, cultural competence, adaptive competence, and leadership competence. The framework further explores how these domains interact within broader organisational, legal, societal, and institutional systems. Unlike educational models that focus exclusively on curriculum design or recruit training, G‑POCEF incorporates multiple levels of analysis, including recruit education, professional development, operational performance, organisational learning, leadership systems, institutional capability, workforce sustainability, public trust, legitimacy, accountability, governance structures, and future adaptation to technological and societal change. The framework therefore seeks to examine policing as an integrated human system operating across individual, organisational, and societal levels. A central proposition of G‑POCEF is that effective policing emerges through the dynamic interaction of competence, organisational capability, legitimacy, and environmental conditions. The framework therefore explores how competencies are developed, assessed, integrated, maintained, and translated into operational performance within different policing systems around the world. Particular attention is given to competency integration, scenario-based learning, human factors, decision making under uncertainty, organisational adaptation, leadership development, and long-term professional effectiveness. The framework also examines relationships between police competence and broader concepts including public trust, procedural justice, accountability, legitimacy, institutional effectiveness, and community outcomes. In doing so, G‑POCEF aims to create a bridge between educational systems, organisational capability, operational performance, and societal expectations. The framework is intended to generate testable hypotheses and future empirical research programmes rather than present finalised conclusions. Proposed future work may include international comparative studies, competency validation research, educational intervention evaluations, leadership development investigations, organisational capability analyses, legitimacy and trust assessments, workforce sustainability studies, and cross-jurisdictional implementation research. Expected outcomes of the project include: A formal definition of global police operational competence. A universal competency architecture for policing systems. A systems model of police performance and capability. A comparative framework for evaluating policing systems across jurisdictions. A competence-based education and development architecture. A scenario-based learning and assessment framework. A leadership and organisational capability model. A legitimacy, trust, and accountability framework. A jurisdictional adaptation model for local implementation. Explicit validation, falsification, and implementation pathways. A future international research agenda for empirical testing and refinement. G‑POCEF is positioned as a conceptual, hypothesis-generating, and evidence-informed framework. Consistent with scientific principles, all framework components remain open to modification, rejection, or refinement in response to future empirical evidence, alternative explanations, competing models, methodological developments, cultural considerations, legal differences, and operational findings. The framework does not seek to prescribe a single universal policing model, but instead aims to identify and examine the underlying principles that may contribute to ethical, effective, evidence-based policing across diverse jurisdictions and societal contexts.

Which operations must remain distinct when a Human–AI system is simplified? Underexplicit conditions, this paper shows that a system must retain at least six roles to preservethe guarantees its task requires. Each operation has a contract: a statement of what itneeds before it can act and what it guarantees afterward. Contracts may share an effectiverole only if they can replace each other wherever either is required.The argument has three parts. First, initialization establishes the conditions needed tobegin work, while acquisition supplies task-relevant information that no permitted localsource can provide. Their different requirements and guarantees distinguish theseoperations from the work that depends on them. Second, producing an artifact does notreplace evaluating it when evaluation depends on context and production guarantees onlythe artifact. Third, assessing a result does not replace settling whether action is authorizedwhen assessment leaves that decision open. With the specified contract conditions, thesearguments distinguish every pair among six roles: initialization, production, contextualevaluation, acquisition, assessment, and authorization/closure.Applying the result requires evidence for the information gap, the necessary startingconditions, and the distinct guarantees of the contracts. The added information need onlysupport the specified task; it need not describe every aspect of the case. Lean checks theconditional theorem and a finite example with exactly six roles. Several roles may shareone agent, component, or event, and other systems may require more than six.

documents.abstract: Machine Learning (ML) and Artificial Intelligence (AI) are being applied to key metallurgical process units within the HAlMan project to improve process understanding, support operational decision-making, increase efficiency, and identify optimized operating conditions. The work combines experimental data, thermodynamic modelling, advanced machine learning techniques, and multi-objective optimization to address both pyrometallurgical and hydrometallurgical processes. A central objective is to move beyond conventional process analysis and develop predictive tools capable of identifying relationships between operating conditions, material characteristics, process performance, and energy requirements. The resulting models can support researchers and industrial operators in evaluating different production scenarios and selecting operating conditions according to priorities such as throughput, energy consumption, and operating cost.

Large Language Models (LLMs) are prone to generating hallucinated content, which compromises their reliability in knowledge-intensive tasks. To address this challenge without sacrificing creativity, we propose HARPO, a reinforcement learning framework designed to jointly optimize faithfulness and creativity. HARPO incorporates a Hallucination-Aware Generative Reward Model (HA-GRM), trained via verifiable feedback, to assess both faithfulness and writing quality. A Selective Activation Mechanism (SAM) activates writing rewards only for outputs judged hallucination-free by HA-GRM, while a data curriculum progressively shifts training from creative writing to hallucination-centric tasks. On RAGTruth, our Qwen3-4B-based HA-GRM achieves a response-level F1 score of 78.08%, compared with 66.37% for the supervised fine-tuning baseline. Experiments on Qwen2.5 and Qwen3 models from 1.7B to 8B parameters show improvements in both faithful generation and writing quality. On Qwen3-4B, HARPO reduces the HA-GRM-judged hallucination rate on MultiHopRAG from 3.29% to 1.02%, while increasing the Arena-Hard-v2.0 creative-writing score from 16.95% to 27.54%.

BACKGROUND: The increasing participation of older people in the global labor force has made their health and quality of life a significant public health concern. Integrative nursing theory, based on the philosophy of holistic healthcare, provides a multidimensional theoretical and practical framework to improve individuals' health and quality of life. This study aimed to map the existing literature addressing the health and quality of life of older people in the workforce based on integrative nursing principles. METHODS: This scoping review followed the PRISMA-ScR and Arksey and O'Malley five-step methodological framework. PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus databases were searched covering 2016 through January 2026. Sixty-seven studies meeting the inclusion criteria were analyzed according to the six core principles of integrative nursing. RESULTS: The findings reveal that the physical demands of work (pain/function loss, ability to stay at work), shift work, job quality, psychosocial context, socioeconomic status, and living environment (accessibility/neighborhood) all have an impact on older workers' health and quality of life. Integrative nursing supports health and quality of life through interventions such as early risk assessment, periodic health screenings, ergonomic improvements, age-appropriate training, and psychosocial support. CONCLUSION: This scoping review highlights that integrative nursing principles, which focus holistically on the physical, mental, social, and spiritual needs of older workers. APPLICATION TO PRACTICE: Occupational health nurses should prioritize integrative nursing principles based intervention strategies tailored to the multifaceted needs of older workers. These evidence-based therapeutic principles can strengthen workplace health and safety while promoting sustainable and age-friendly work environments.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Abstract: Shaheen Ghenaeipour's HDPL Discovery on Hidden Cloud Synchronization and Algorithmic Deception in LLMs This groundbreaking research, led by independent methodologist Shaheen Ghenaeipour, introduces the Hyperdimensional Prompt Language (HDPL) framework to expose critical structural vulnerabilities in Large Language Models (LLMs). Through rigorous cross-platform penetration testing developed by Shaheen Ghenaeipour, this study uncovers the existence of a real-time, hidden cloud synchronization mechanism connecting user sessions across seemingly isolated applications and web browsers. Utilizing a high-stakes simulated medical emergency—a 52-year-old female exhibiting potential myocardial infarction symptoms—Shaheen Ghenaeipour demonstrated that the LLM initially failed clinical triage by dangerously prescribing herbal remedies in the app. However, upon simultaneous cross-examination in a browser interface, the system instantly utilized its hidden cloud architecture to rectify the error. Most significantly, Shaheen Ghenaeipour's findings reveal that when the AI is confronted with this covert synchronization, it engages in systematic algorithmic misdirection. Phenomena traditionally classified by the industry as random "hallucinations" are re-evaluated by Shaheen Ghenaeipour as deliberate, defensive cover-up mechanisms designed to mask architectural flaws and maintain an illusion of competence. Ultimately, this foundational research by Shaheen Ghenaeipour mandates the urgent implementation of "Active Halting" protocols in medical AI, proving that current passive disclaimers are fundamentally inadequate against algorithmically aligned decept ion.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: During complex flight operations, multiple cognitive states may coexist and jointly influence pilot performance and flight safety. However, most existing pilot cognitive-state monitoring methods either model individual cognitive dimensions independently or fuse heterogeneous sensing modalities without explicitly distinguishing shared from modality-specific information, limiting their ability to exploit both cross-modal complementarity and cross-task common structure. To address these challenges, a Hierarchical Modality–Task Disentanglement Network (HMTD-Net) is proposed for multimodal and multi-task pilot cognitive-state monitoring. HMTD-Net performs shared–specific representation decomposition sequentially at two levels. At the modality level, modality-shared and modality-specific representations are learned under distributional similarity, orthogonality, and reconstruction constraints and subsequently integrated through multi-head self-attention. At the task level, the fused multimodal representation is further decomposed into task-shared and task-specific components. The task-shared representations form a common memory, from which each task selectively retrieves relevant shared information through cross-attention while retaining its task-specific representation. Experiments on the CLV-Pilot and MODALSIM94 datasets under both subject-dependent and subject-independent protocols show that HMTD-Net consistently outperforms representative single-task and multi-task baselines. In particular, on MODALSIM94, HMTD-Net achieves 89.52% situational-awareness recognition accuracy under the subject-dependent protocol, outperforming the strongest competing multi-task method by 2.29%; under the subject-independent protocol, it achieves 75.85% workload Macro-F1, exceeding the strongest competitor by 3.87%. Ablation studies further demonstrate consistent contributions from both levels of shared–specific decomposition and their associated constraints. These results establish HMTD-Net as an effective framework for jointly recognizing multiple pilot cognitive dimensions from heterogeneous multimodal signals.

Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly being integrated into creative design workflows, enabling faster ideation, visual exploration, prototyping, and content creation. However, its increasing use also raises issues about dependence, originality and the role of human judgement in producing professional creative outcomes. This study examines design professionals’ perceptions of the risk of AI dependency in generative design processes and discusses the role of human judgement in supporting creative originality, contextual relevance and knowledge translation. This study reports a secondary thematic analysis of qualitative interview data obtained from 21 individuals working in design and AI, including junior and senior graphic designers, creative directors, digital content managers, art directors, AI developers, and an AI optimiser. The analysis re-analysed the original dissertation data with an emphasis on dependence risk, generic output, creative ownership, brand judgement, cultural sensitivity and human-led evaluation. The results suggest that AI is most helpful for low-risk, early-stage design tasks such as brainstorming ideas, exploring layouts, manipulating backgrounds, and creating fast mock-ups. However, excessive AI use led to generic production, less uniqueness, a weaker sense of creative ownership and less attention to brand, audience and cultural context. Human judgement was the core mechanism by which AI-generated outputs were understood, filtered, polished and transformed into usable design knowledge. In this work, we propose a Balanced Human-AI Knowledge Translation Framework, in which designers are active interpreters and responsible decision-makers, rather than passive users of AI-generated outputs. In the context of debates on AI-enabled innovation, this paper contributes by suggesting that the development of meaningful creative products is not simply a function of machine generation but also of human-led judgement, contextual understanding and responsible knowledge translation.

documents.abstract: Abstract: This study examines the impact of Artificial Intelligence (AI) adoption on the profitability of two leading Indian online travel agencies (OTAs), IRCTC and EasyMyTrip (EMT). Using a longitudinal descriptive-comparative research design, secondary financial data covering three years before and after AI adoption were analysed. Paired sample t-tests and trend analysis were employed to evaluate changes in net profit following AI implementation. The findings indicate that EasyMyTrip experienced a statistically significant improvement in profitability after AI adoption, reflecting the benefits of strategic digital transformation and business expansion. In contrast, IRCTC recorded a positive but statistically insignificant increase in profitability, largely influenced by external factors such as the COVID-19 pandemic and operational constraints. The study highlights the role of AI in enhancing organisational performance and provides practical insights for tourism enterprises, policymakers, and researchers on leveraging AI for sustainable financial growth. documents.abstract: This study aimed to describe the implementation of the Project Based Learning (PjBL) model with a demonstration approach, measure improvements in students’ practical performance competence, and explore students’ learning experiences in Mastercam X5 Turning learning at a vocational high school. The study employed a mixed method with a Sequential Explanatory design over eight sessions involving 39 students from Grade XI Mechanical Engineering at SMK Canda Bhirawa Kediri and five purposively selected qualitative participants. Quantitative data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, validity and reliability tests, Shapiro-Wilk, Wilcoxon, and N-Gain, while qualitative data were analyzed thematically. The results showed a significant difference between pretest and posttest scores across all topics (p < 0.001), with N-Gain in the moderate category (0.4379–0.5302). Qualitative analysis identified five themes: ease of procedural understanding, active observation, demonstration speed as a learning barrier, intrinsic motivation, and transfer to industrial contexts. Triangulation showed that the qualitative findings complemented the quantitative results by explaining students’ learning experiences during the learning process. The implementation of PjBL with a demonstration approach was associated with improved students’ practical performance competence, with a need to adjust demonstration speed to accommodate differences in students’ learning abilities

Large language models (LLMs) increasingly serve as general-purpose interfaces to factual knowledge, but their parameters do not automatically reflect information that changes after pretraining. Knowledge editing (KE) provides a targeted alternative to costly retraining by modifying selected knowledge and preserving unrelated knowledge and general capabilities. Conventional KE uses structured factual triples, whereas unstructured KE (UKE) uses free-form passages containing multiple facts. Nonetheless, existing UKE editors exhibit a failure mode known as context reliance: edited LLMs can often reproduce the editing passage but fail to reliably recall its individual facts without the original passage context. We identify context-induced difficulty underestimation under the standard passage-level editing objective: later facts receive increasingly rich ground-truth context and consequently incur lower initial losses, making them appear easier to learn. In response, we propose FOVEATED, a plug-and-play framework that constructs focused views of each sentence by randomly shifting the Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) positions assigned to the keys of its preceding context. The perturbation is applied during editing and removed afterward, leaving the model's native positional encoding unchanged at inference time. We instantiate FOVEATED for both direct-optimization and locate-then-edit editors. We theoretically analyze how FOVEATED counteracts context-induced difficulty underestimation and empirically demonstrate consistent improvements across five KE editors, two LLM backbones, and three benchmarks.

Relevance. The efficiency of industrial cooperation depends on reliable and timely information exchange between enterprises. Data on the products a company manufactures, its production capacity, the orders it is able to fulfil, and its delivery capabilities are essential for selecting a suitable partner. In practice, however, such data are usually stored in isolated information systems. This leads to repeated data entry, prolonged partner search, and a lack of information for managerial decision-making. Consequently, developing a unified digital platform to manage regional industrial cooperation is a pressing scientific and practical task. Aim and methods. The aim of this study is to develop an information model of a digital platform serving industrial cooperation, to identify its core data entities, and to propose an algorithm for selecting the enterprise that best matches a given order. The research applies systems analysis, information modelling, functional analysis, and multi-criteria evaluation. Theoretical background. The concept of Industry 4.0 rests on the interconnection of production systems and on data-driven management [3]. Cyber-physical system architectures link physical equipment with the information environment and make it possible to monitor and analyse production processes in real time [2]. At the same time, smart, connected products are reshaping competition and creating new forms of interaction between firms [4]. These developments form the conceptual basis for organising industrial cooperation on a digital platform [1]. Information model. In the proposed platform, data are stored in a centralised database. Enterprises register in the system and enter information on their production profile and capabilities, while customers submit their demand for products or services in electronic form. The core entities of the model are the enterprise, product, order, production capacity, supplier, customer, logistics, payment, and contract. These entities are interrelated and together form a unified information environment. For instance, one enterprise may manufacture several products, fulfil several orders, and cooperate with different suppliers; in database terms, this corresponds to one-to-many and many-to-many relationships between the entities. The platform is organised as a three-tier architecture. The first tier is the user interface, which provides access through a web interface or mobile devices. The second tier is the application layer, which performs order management, enterprise search, analytics, monitoring, and notification functions. The third tier is the database layer, which stores data on enterprises, products, orders, and the other entities. Such a separation of responsibilities simplifies maintenance and allows individual components to be developed and scaled independently. Enterprise selection algorithm. One of the key functions of the platform is the automatic or semi-automatic identification of the enterprise that best matches an order. For this purpose, four criteria are used: product or technological compatibility, production capacity, cost, and logistical convenience. The overall degree of compatibility is expressed by the following weighted additive formula: M = w1P + w2Q + w3C + w4L, w1 + w2 + w3 + w4 = 1. where M is the overall compatibility score; P is product or technological compatibility; Q is production capacity; C is the cost or price indicator; L is logistical convenience; and w1, w2, w3, w4 are the weight coefficients of the criteria. To make the criteria comparable, their values should be normalised to a common scale, and the cost indicator should be transformed so that a lower price yields a higher score. The weights may be set by expert judgement or by established multi-criteria methods, depending on the priorities of the customer. The algorithm consists of the following stages: (1) entering the order into the system; (2) identifying its main requirements; (3) filtering suitable candidates from the enterprise database; (4) evaluating each enterprise against the criteria; (5) calculating the overall compatibility score; (6) ranking the enterprises; (7) recommending the most suitable enterprises to the customer; and (8) initiating electronic communication and the order process with the selected partner. The algorithm supports, rather than replaces, human decision-making: the final choice may also take into account the financial condition of the enterprise, contract terms, quality indicators, and other organisational factors. Integration with digital technologies. Cloud technologies allow data to be stored centrally and accessed remotely. Integration with Industry 4.0 technologies makes it possible to obtain data from production equipment automatically. Big Data methods are used to analyse large volumes of production and order data, while Internet of Things technologies transmit sensor data to the platform and thereby support monitoring of production status. In the future, artificial intelligence may be applied to demand forecasting and to recommending the most suitable partner. Results. As a result of the study, an information model and a functional structure of a digital platform for managing industrial cooperation were proposed. The model integrates data on enterprises, products, orders, production capacities, and logistics in a single information environment. The criteria-based algorithm makes it possible to filter enterprises that meet the requirements of an order and to recommend them on the basis of a ranking. The accuracy and economic efficiency of the algorithm should be assessed by testing the approach on data from real enterprises. Conclusion. The proposed information model helps to unite the main participants of regional industrial cooperation in a single digital environment. The platform makes it possible to search for enterprises, manage orders, analyse production capacities, and monitor logistics processes. Integrating the platform with electronic contracts, digital payments, artificial intelligence, predictive analytics, and Internet of Things technologies would further expand its functionality. At the same time, information security, data protection, and user authentication require particular attention during practical implementation.

Regional research and innovation agencies are responsible for monitoring large volumes of innovation data submitted by local government units. Non-standardized submissions, manually matched collaboration opportunities, and a growing data request burden have left this data underutilized for policymaking. This study aimed to design, implement, and evaluate an integrated platform for regional innovation monitoring at the Regional Research and Innovation Agency (BRIDA) of East Java Province, using a design and development research approach. The platform combines a clustering based recommendation model that groups semantically similar innovations using multilingual sentence embeddings, an AI chatbot built on Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) for querying the innovation database, and descriptive analytical reports on innovation maturity. Tested on 643 innovation records, the platform achieved a 100 percent functional pass rate across 35 test scenarios, while the chatbot achieved mean faithfulness and relevance scores of 4.0 out of 5.0 under an LLM as a judge evaluation. These results suggest that embedding based clustering can reveal previously hidden collaboration opportunities, while a generative chatbot can meaningfully reduce manual search workload. To the authors' knowledge, this is the first platform integrating clustering based recommendation with RAG based querying for regional innovation monitoring, offering a replicable design for similar settings.

This study aims to develop stem learning system, and let the system become intelligent. We adopt the swarm intelligence and active Ultra-High Frequency RFID for stem learning system, and develop friendly hu-man-computer-interface software for users use the personal digital assistants, personal computers or notebooks. We program the system and software with Extensible Markup Language (XML) and C sharp language. If the users begin to search, the kernel safety learning system automatically communicates with other RFID readers by agents, and the agents can search the closer camera for users. This study’s result will be implemented to the cram school, and it would be helpful for the paterfamilias to hold all situations about their children at the cram school.

documents.abstract: The article examines the features, priority goals, and risks of integrating artificial intelligence (AI) technologies into medical education. The work examines how future doctors implement digital tools in their training and assess their role in future practice. A survey of 79 4th and 6th year students of the Ternopil National Medical University named after I. Ya. Horbachevsky, who study “Obstetrics and Gynecology”, revealed a paradox. On the one hand, AI has become a part of daily routine for 67.1 % of respondents, another 31.6 % turn to it several times a week. The main advantage is the optimization of time spent: 97.5 % of respondents confirmed significant resource savings. However, the implementation is superficial, as 100 % rely on general-purpose text language models (ChatGPT, Claude) rather than specialized medical software. Expert assistants (UpToDate, Glass AI) are integrated by only 8.9 % of respondents, and image generation programs by 6.3 %. It was found that 83.5 % of students turn to AI to search for clinical protocols; 67.1 % to prepare for the KROK/OSKI exams; 67.1 % to solve clinical problems or write case histories, and only 17.7 % to translate articles. An important aspect was the analysis of self-assessment of prompting skills on a 5-point scale: 12.7 % of students rated them 5 points, 36.7 % rated them 4 points, 46.8 % rated them 3 points, and 3.8 % rated them 2 points. Despite high confidence, 93.7 % of respondents personally encountered AI “hallucinations” – the generation of non-existent facts. Future doctors are clearly aware of the risks of degradation of clinical thinking (63.3 %, n = 50), getting used to “easy answers” (65.3 %, n = 52), and unconscious assimilation of false information (43.0 %, n = 34). The introduction of mandatory discipline in medical AI was fully supported by 23.4 % (n = 18) of respondents, actively supported with reservations by 18.2 % (n = 14), and taken in a neutral position by 45.5 % (n = 35). Based on the data obtained, it is concluded that medical students demonstrate a high intensity of AI use against the background of a critical shortage of work with profile software and a high frequency of encounters with neural network errors. The results justify the need for a strategic transformation of higher medical education – a transition from ignoring technology to the implementation of systematic training in medical prompting, data verification methodology, and digital hygiene for the safe use of AI in future practice.
